## Story you tell yourself in 60 seconds

Read this aloud. Twice. The dates are not bullet points — they are characters in a sentence that keeps going. The brain remembers a story.

::: {.smallstory}

**In 1948, a state was born and another was broken** — the Nakba. *(That's the founding rupture. Hold it.)*

**In 1967, six days changed the map** — Israel took the West Bank, Gaza, the Sinai, and the Golan. The Arab states' credibility cracked, and the Palestinians began to come back into history on their own terms.

**In 1979, Sadat shook a hand and changed everything** — the Egyptian-Israeli peace treaty broke the pan-Arab consensus and *delinked* the Palestinian question from Egyptian leverage.

**In 1993, three men stood on the South Lawn** — Rabin, Clinton, Arafat — and Oslo created a Palestinian quasi-state by deferring every hard question for five years. The five years became forever.

**In 2020, the price of peace changed** — the Abraham Accords swapped "a Palestinian state" for "Iran-deterrence and economic upside." The Saudis didn't sign.

**On December 8, 2024, Damascus fell** — Iran's land bridge to Hezbollah severed. The carousel kept turning, but with one less rider.

:::

```{=html}
<aside class="recite-aloud">
  <h4>Recite this in 30 seconds</h4>
  <p class="rhyme">
    <strong>Forty-eight</strong>: born and broken ·
    <strong>Sixty-seven</strong>: six-day shock ·
    <strong>Seventy-nine</strong>: Sadat shakes hands ·
    <strong>Ninety-three</strong>: Oslo on the lawn ·
    <strong>Twenty-twenty</strong>: the price flips ·
    <strong>Twelve-eight twenty-four</strong>: Damascus down.
  </p>
  <p class="hum">Six beats. Repeat three times. The rhythm is the memory.</p>
</aside>
```

## The hand mnemonic

You have ten fingers. You only need six. Six dates, six fingers — and they are *in order*, left to right, just like the timeline.

```{=html}
<div class="hand-mnemonic">
  <div class="hand-row">
    <div class="finger"><div class="finger-label">RIGHT THUMB</div><div class="finger-year">1948</div><div class="finger-tag">Born &amp; broken</div></div>
    <div class="finger"><div class="finger-label">RIGHT INDEX</div><div class="finger-year">1967</div><div class="finger-tag">Six-day shock</div></div>
    <div class="finger"><div class="finger-label">RIGHT MIDDLE</div><div class="finger-year">1979</div><div class="finger-tag">Sadat shakes</div></div>
    <div class="finger"><div class="finger-label">RIGHT RING</div><div class="finger-year">1993</div><div class="finger-tag">Oslo on lawn</div></div>
    <div class="finger"><div class="finger-label">RIGHT PINKY</div><div class="finger-year">2020</div><div class="finger-tag">Price flips</div></div>
    <div class="finger left-thumb"><div class="finger-label">LEFT THUMB</div><div class="finger-year">12·8·24</div><div class="finger-tag">Damascus down</div></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

If your mind blanks in the room: put your right hand on the desk, look down, and tap each finger. The story comes back.

## Three frames, three vivid images

Drop the four. Three is enough. Each one is a single picture you carry with you.

```{=html}
<div class="three-frames">
  <div class="vivid-frame">
    <div class="frame-emoji">🛡️</div>
    <h3>Bellin → Bouncers</h3>
    <p class="frame-year">2004</p>
    <p>Picture <strong>bouncers at the door of an Arab regime</strong> — military, secret police, riot police. The regime survives because of who's at the door, not because anyone loves it. <em>Use this for any "why didn't the Arab Spring work" question.</em></p>
  </div>
  <div class="vivid-frame">
    <div class="frame-emoji">⛽</div>
    <h3>Mitchell → Mineral</h3>
    <p class="frame-year">2011</p>
    <p>Picture a <strong>black pipeline running under the region</strong>. Coal democratized labor. Oil concentrates power. The MENA region is "the most-penetrated subsystem" because of those pipes. <em>Use this for any US power / sanctions / structural-critique question.</em></p>
  </div>
  <div class="vivid-frame">
    <div class="frame-emoji">🤝</div>
    <h3>Goodarzi → Glue</h3>
    <p class="frame-year">2006</p>
    <p>Picture <strong>Iran and Syria glued together</strong> — by mutual threat, not by sect. Someone whispers "they're allies because both are Shia"; you shake your head. It was always strategy. <em>Use this for Iran-Syria, axis of resistance, or December 2024 collapse.</em></p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.callout-tip}
**One more, only if you have time:** *Beinin* — "history and categories of knowledge." If the prompt asks about the New Historians or 1948 historiography, drop his name and that exact phrase.
:::

## One thesis sentence (four fill-in slots)

This sentence works for almost any prompt. The four highlighted words are the only things you adapt to the specific question.

::: {.fillthesis}
> "In 2026, the Arab-Israeli conflict has been reshaped by **[1967]** — *the founding shock* — through **[1979]** — *Egypt's defection* — and **[1993]** — *Oslo's deferral* — leaving **[a Palestinian question]** that is more central to the regional system than ever before, and less solvable than at any moment since 1948."
:::

You can substitute the bracketed terms. For example, if the prompt is about the Abraham Accords, you'd write *"by the API of 2002, the Abraham Accords of 2020, and the post-Oct-7 freeze, leaving a Palestinian question..."*

The structure stays. The words flex.

## One counterargument move

Every essay needs a moment where you say "one might object…" and then beat the objection. **Memorize this exact sentence.** It works against almost any objection.

::: {.fillthesis style="border-left-color:#555;background:rgba(85,85,85,.06);"}
> *"One might object that this account overweights structure and underweights agency. The objection is partly right — structural openings don't close themselves — but the deeper point is that each rupture changed what agency could accomplish, which is why the same actors produce different outcomes at different moments."*
:::

That's it. One paragraph. Beats almost any "but what about X" question.

## One closer (drop this as the last sentence)

::: {.fillthesis style="border-left-color:#2e7d32;background:rgba(46,125,50,.06);"}
> *"This is part of the unfinished business Hammad's lectures returned to — the question of how a regional system absorbs structural change without resolving its founding ruptures."*
:::

That sentence signals you read his slides. He'll see it. **Don't skip it.**

## If you blank in the room

Three reset moves, in order:

1. **Stop writing.** Put the pen down. Look at the desk for ten seconds.
2. **Tap your right thumb.** Say "1948 — born and broken." Then your index — "1967 — six-day shock." The whole story comes back through your hand.
3. **Write *one* sentence on the page** — any sentence, even just *"This question is really about [something]."* The first sentence breaks the freeze.

## Memorize check (90 seconds)

```{=html}
<ol class="memo-check">
  <li>Recite the 6-date story aloud, in order.</li>
  <li>Recite the rhythmic cadence: "Forty-eight: born and broken · Sixty-seven: six-day shock · Seventy-nine: Sadat shakes hands · Ninety-three: Oslo on the lawn · Twenty-twenty: price flips · Twelve-eight twenty-four: Damascus down."</li>
  <li>Tap your right hand: thumb 1948, index 1967, middle 1979, ring 1993, pinky 2020 · left thumb 12·8·24.</li>
  <li>Name the three frames: <strong>Bouncers · Mineral · Glue</strong>.</li>
  <li>Say the thesis sentence aloud, swapping in the four bracketed terms.</li>
  <li>Say the closer: "This is part of the unfinished business…"</li>
</ol>
```

If you can do all six in 90 seconds, you have what you need. Walk in.
